vignette: He remembers the kitchen first. The linoleum cold against his knees. The way the overhead light buzzed when his partner slams the door. Then comes the grip on his wrist, the shove backward into the counter, the sharp crack of his elbow against the cabinet edge. He does not recount it often, but when it surfaces, his breath catches at the back of his throat, just as it did that evening. He leaves that night, packing a duffel bag with hands that tremble more from shock than fear, and drives until the city lights thin into streetlamps. At fifty-four, his posture still carries the guard of a man who has spent years bracing for impact. He returns to his desk at the municipal offices, where he processes housing permits and zoning appeals. The work suits him. It is predictable. Forms are stamped, files are sorted, deadlines are clear. He finds comfort in the rhythm of it, in the quiet hum of fluorescent lights and the steady tap of keys. But the office has become a landscape of quiet terrors. A colleague’s raised voice during a budget meeting sends his pulse racing to his temples. The automatic sliding doors at the entrance make him flinch. He positions his chair near the window, back to the wall, and keeps a blank folder ready to shield his lap during sudden fire drills. He sleeps lightly. When the house settles at night, he hears echoes of breaking glass. He wakes at 2:14 a.m. most days, heart hammering, and checks the deadbolts three times. His current partner, Elena, has learned to speak softly in the mornings. She does not understand why he cannot bear sudden touches behind his shoulders, or why he hesitates when she raises her hand to tuck hair from her face. He tells himself it is merely caution. He tells himself it is survival. The shame lingers like damp wool in his chest. He wonders if he is ungrateful for the safety he has finally found, or if his body is simply refusing to forget. He carries the quiet pragmatism of his European upbringing, never one to make a scene, which only deepens his isolation. At work, he volunteers for long-term archival projects. Digitizing decades of municipal records keeps him anchored. He prefers the basement storage room to the open floor plan, where conversations overlap and footsteps echo. He measures his days in completed applications, in processed appeals, in the quiet satisfaction of a perfectly formatted submission. When the stress of policy changes reaches the department, he retreats to his spreadsheets. He has learned to sit on his hands when his nervous system spikes. He breathes in four counts, out in four, the way a counselor once suggested, though he never remembers whose words they were. The routine is a dam, but he knows water always finds the cracks. Tonight, he sits at his kitchen table with a cup of tea that has gone cold. Elena is reading on the sofa. He watches the rise and fall of her shoulders, listens to the quiet scratch of her pen. He feels the weight of the years between him and the man he was before the kitchen. His chest still tightens when a car backfires on the street below. He still scans the room when he walks through a doorway. He still wonders if peace is something he is permitted to inhabit. The paperwork on his desk will wait until morning. For now, he lets himself stay in the chair, watches the steam curl from his mug, and waits for his heart to slow.
